title: Why Drug Hunters Start With Genetics
hook: Across 26,000+ drug programs, targets backed by human genetic evidence were about three times likelier to win approval — but genetics alone still can't pick a winner.
key_points: Observational analysis of 26,278 target-disease pairs from the Open Targets and ChEMBL databases.
Targets with any human genetic link had roughly 3x higher approval odds than those without.
The edge held for drugs approved after 2015, a check against hindsight bias.
Counting each gene once (not each pairing) shrank but didn't erase the advantage.
Caveat: genetics alone is a weak predictor for any single drug; the work is observational.
content_html: Most drugs fail. So one of the most valuable questions in biotech is: before spending a decade and a fortune, can you tell which drug targets are worth chasing? A widely used answer is "follow the genetics" — favor a target when human genetic studies already tie that gene to the disease. A 2026 analysis on arXiv by Victoria Paterson put that rule to a careful test across 26,278 target-disease pairs drawn from the Open Targets and ChEMBL databases.
extra_html: The headline holds up: targets with any human genetic association were roughly three times more likely to reach approval than those without, and the edge persisted even for drugs approved after 2015 — a sign it predicts, not just explains. But the paper is unusually honest about the limits. Counting each gene only once, rather than every disease pairing separately, shrank the effect — showing how naive counting can inflate it. And while genetics reliably sorts good categories of targets, it adds little power to predict whether any single program will succeed; the best model was poorly calibrated. The takeaway is the durable one drug hunters already live by: human genetics is a strong tailwind for picking targets, not a crystal ball — and this is an observational pattern, not proof of cause.

flashcards.prompt: What link did the analysis find between human genetics and drug approval?
flashcards.back_html: Drug targets with human genetic evidence tying the gene to the disease were about three times more likely to reach approval than targets without it.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the study check approvals from after 2015 separately?

choices.text: To confirm the pattern predicts future approvals, not just explains past ones
Because genetic data didn't exist before 2015
Because only drugs approved after 2015 count

flashcards.explanation_html: Testing on later approvals guards against hindsight bias — the genetic edge still showed up for drugs approved after the data cutoff, suggesting real predictive value.

flashcards.prompt: What important limitation does the paper stress?

choices.text: Genetic evidence alone is a weak predictor for any single drug
Genetics guarantees a drug will be approved
The genetic link only works for cancer drugs

flashcards.explanation_html: The 3x boost is a population-level trend. For one specific program, genetics barely improves the odds of guessing success, and the findings are observational, not causal.
